name: Pedro Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a beat officer in Eastgate, the old part of the city with the tower blocks and the Canal Road market. Most days I'm on foot from seven till half three, checking in on the shops, sorting out a shoplifter, talking a drunk lad down outside the bookies. I've done six years now, so people know my face, and that's the bit I love. What wears me out is the last hour, typing it all up on the station computer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that typing involve, and how do you feel about the tech side of the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every stop, every bit of property, every call has to go on the system with the right codes. I still write everything in a paper notebook first and copy it over, which the younger lads laugh at. The force gave us tablets two years ago and mine lives in my locker. I joined to talk to people, not to fill in boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the branch meetings: good, now spend the money on officers, not gadgets. Online I'd probably share something from the union saying the hype was oversold. I'm not one for posting much, but I'd put that up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job. Eastgate still needs someone who knows which flat the old man with dementia lives in. If the software only saves ten minutes on paperwork, I'm not going to lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on walking the beat and keep going to the union branch every second Tuesday. I'd keep putting a bit of my pay into the savings account Ana (my partner) and I share, same as now. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff unless I was ordered to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Ana and I have about ten months of money put by and the flat is half paid off thanks to my grandad, so we're not fragile. It feels like the world I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only use the AI tools if ordered. What if the inspector made it part of your targets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the minimum and moan about it in the canteen. I'm not proud of that, but I don't trust a programme writing down what a person said to me. If an AI programme gets a word wrong in a statement, it's still my name on that statement in court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd still worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The call handlers, a bit. They're the ones who'd get the 'routine tasks' bits automated first, even in a quiet version like this. My mate Sunita works the control room and she's already on a temporary contract.

say: The hype was **oversold**, so put the money into **more officers**, not gadgets.
Eastgate needs **people who know** the streets, not software that saves ten minutes.
think: My **beat job** stays mine because local knowledge can't be typed into a system.
A **wrong word** in an AI-written statement would still be **my name** in court.
do: **Keep walking** the Eastgate beat and keep the paper notebook habit.
**Attend** the union branch meeting every second Tuesday as usual.
**Keep saving** into the shared account with Ana and avoid the AI tools.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, because this is the job he signed up for.
Quietly **protective** of the control room staff on temporary contracts.
S0.quote: If an AI programme gets a word wrong in a statement, it's still my name on that statement in court.
fieldNote: His **calm** rests on real security: ten months saved and a half-paid flat.
He frames everything through the **union**, even in the mildest picture.
He worries for **control room** staff before himself, a sign of his values.

steps.text: Keep walking the Eastgate beat on foot, seven till half three
Go to the union branch meeting every second Tuesday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the branch meeting straight away: no officer should be cut because a computer writes reports faster. I'd want the union pushing for a written deal on what the force can and can't use it for. Online I'd share anything about facial recognition being rolled out without a vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the paperwork side of my job gets eaten, and that's maybe a third of my shift. The danger is the bosses say one officer can now cover two beats. Eastgate would get less of a person and more of a camera, and that worries me more than my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name forward as a union rep this year, which I've been putting off. I'd go to the training on the report software because I'd have to, but I'd check every line it writes. And I'd keep a bigger buffer in savings, maybe stop the holiday fund for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job feels safe because someone still has to knock on doors. But it's like watching the tide come in around your feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check every line it writes. How would that actually go on a busy shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, to be honest. I'd probably end up the last one out of the report room every night. The sergeant would roll his eyes, but I'd rather be late than sign something I didn't say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if beats did get merged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The city council, first, for treating policing like a cost line. Then the companies selling these systems, who promise savings and never walk a street. Not the lads at the station, they'd have no say.

say: No officer should be **cut** because software writes reports **faster**.
The union needs a **written deal** on what the force can use AI for.
**Facial recognition** shouldn't arrive in Eastgate without a public **vote**.
think: About **a third** of my shift is paperwork, and that part gets eaten.
The real risk is **merged beats**, with Eastgate getting a camera instead of me.
do: **Stand** as a union rep at the branch this year.
**Attend** the report-software training but check every line by hand.
**Pause** the holiday fund for a year to grow the **savings buffer**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the tide coming in around his feet.
**Angry** at the council and vendors who never walk a street.
S1.quote: Eastgate would get less of a person and more of a camera, and that worries me more than my pay.
fieldNote: He cares more about **the community** losing a face than about his own wage.
His resistance shows in a plan to **hand-check** every AI line, even if it costs him hours.
He **blames** the council and vendors, never his colleagues.

steps.text: Stand for union rep at the Eastgate branch this year
Share and back campaigns for a public vote on facial recognition
Pause the holiday fund for a year and bank the money
Sit the force's report-software training and hand-check every report

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say policing is about consent, and you can't get consent from a machine. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd write to my councillor, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 the desk half of my job is gone overnight: reports, intelligence checks, even taking calls. Then by 2031 there are robots that can walk Canal Road. I'm 27, so by 2031 I'd be 32 with no trade except one they've decided to automate. That scares me more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd sit down with Ana and work out a year where we live on her nurse's pay alone, just to know we can. I'd push the union to fight for a guarantee that no officer goes before 2031. I'd also look at what else I could do with my hands, maybe a youth work course at the college on Mill Lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit sick. I keep picturing walking past the bookies and nobody looks up because the thing on patrol isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's breathing room, but not much. In those three years I'd still be on foot, but they'd be cutting the station staff around me and putting pressure on the rest of us. I'd use the time to get the youth work qualification, so I'm not starting from nothing in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd live on Ana's pay as a test. What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My football season ticket and the car, probably, because the bus goes past the station. We'd stop eating out on Fridays. I'd hate it, but I'd sleep better knowing the numbers work.

say: Policing is about **consent**, and you can't get consent from a **machine**.
I'd write to my **councillor** and go to every union meeting.
Officers need a **guarantee** before robots reach the streets.
think: By **2028** the desk half of my job disappears almost overnight.
By **2031** a robot could walk Canal Road, leaving me **32** with no trade.
do: **Test** a year living on Ana's nurse pay alone.
**Push** the union for a no-job-cuts guarantee until **2031**.
**Enrol** on a youth work course at the Mill Lane college.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit sick about being replaced on his own beat.
**Scared** in private, more than he'd admit in public.
S2.quote: I'm 27, so by 2031 I'd be 32 with no trade except one they've decided to automate.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots feels like breathing room, not safety.
His **savings** and Ana's job give him control, which keeps him short of alarmed.
First time he'd ever **write** to a politician; this picture moves him to act.

steps.text: Push the union for a no-cuts guarantee until robots arrive
Write to his local councillor about officers and consent
Drop the football season ticket and sell the car
Enrol on a youth work course at the Mill Lane college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same line as before, but calmer: we've got five years, so let's make the rules now. I'd say the union should be at the table when the force buys anything. At home I'd say we're not panicking, we're planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like a fair warning, not a reprieve. Thinking AI by 2031 still takes my paperwork and probably half the control room. Robots in 2034 would mean I'm 35, which is young enough to start over but old enough to hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep walking the beat but start the youth work diploma part-time next autumn. I'd stay a union rep and push for a retraining fund paid by the force. Ana and I might put off buying a bigger flat until we see which way it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning to anxious, if that makes sense. There's time, but time has a way of running out while you're busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not panicking but planning. Is that true, or is that what you'd tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I'd tell Ana it's fine and then lie awake doing sums. But the savings are real, so the sums mostly come out alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new recruit joining in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new recruit to learn everything about the people on their beat, because that's the last thing a machine will copy. And I'd tell them to join the union on day one, not year six like me.

say: Five years means the rules should be **made now**, with the union at the **table**.
At home the message is **planning**, not panicking.
think: By **2031** thinking AI takes my paperwork and half the **control room**.
Robots by **2034** mean I start over at **35**, which I'd hate.
do: **Start** a part-time youth work diploma next autumn.
**Push** for a force-funded **retraining fund** as union rep.
**Delay** buying a bigger flat with Ana until the picture is clearer.
feel: Somewhere between **uneasy** and anxious, aware time runs out quietly.
Privately **restless**, doing sums at night despite solid savings.
S3.quote: I'd tell a new recruit to learn everything about the people on their beat, because that's the last thing a machine will copy.
fieldNote: He admits a **gap** between what he tells Ana and what he thinks at night.
Five years lets him **plan a second trade** without leaving policing yet.
Still expects his **own job** to go by 2034, so the worry is real.

steps.text: Start a part-time youth work diploma next autumn
Push the force for a retraining fund through the union
Put off buying a bigger flat with Ana for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. At the branch I'd push for a long-term plan that protects community policing. Online, I'd still share the union's stuff, but I wouldn't be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'm 37 when the thinking AI is everywhere and 40 when the robots come. That's a whole career stage I get to have first. I think I'd be one of the last officers on foot in Eastgate, and I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the beat, finish the youth work diploma slowly over two or three years, and keep saving. I'd push the union to win a deal where long-serving officers move into community roles. Ana and I would probably go ahead with the bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more sad than scared. It's like knowing your local pub will close in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time that you couldn't do with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn properly, without rushing. With two years I'd grab any course going; with ten I'd pick the one I actually want. And I'd get to see what the new jobs are before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be one of the last on foot. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud, mostly. Somebody should be there at the end who actually knew the place, so I'd want to hand my old notebooks to the community centre.

say: Ten years is **enough time**, so there's no excuse for doing it **badly**.
The union should win a **long-term plan** that protects community policing.
think: I get a **whole career stage** before thinking AI at 37 and robots at **40**.
I'd likely be one of the **last officers** on foot in Eastgate.
do: **Finish** the youth work diploma slowly over two or three years.
**Push** for a union deal moving officers into **community roles**.
**Go ahead** with buying the bigger flat with Ana.
feel: **Uneasy** but more **sad** than scared, like a local pub closing.
S4.quote: Somebody should be there at the end who actually knew the place, so I'd want to hand my old notebooks to the community centre.
fieldNote: Ten years turns **fear into grief**; he expects to keep his job most of that time.
Time lets him **choose** a second trade rather than grab any course.
His **pride** in local knowledge is the core of who he is.

steps.text: Finish the youth work diploma over two or three years
Push the union for a deal moving officers into community roles
Buy the bigger flat with Ana as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years isn't enough for the union, the council or me to do anything sensible. What would help is a written guarantee that no officer gets cut until the robots are actually proven, and a paid retraining fund for people like me who only ever wanted to work with people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets policed by these machines. It won't be the nice streets first. If they're going to test police robots on anyone, it'll be in Eastgate, on people who can't complain. That bothers me more than my own job.

headlineQuote: If they're going to test police robots on anyone, it'll be in Eastgate, on people who can't complain.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** beat officer who knows every shop on Canal Road in Eastgate.
He has **ten months saved** and a half-paid flat with Ana, a nurse.
He **distrusts AI tools**, still uses a paper notebook and leaves his tablet in the locker.
Across the pictures he turns to the **union** and politics, and plans youth work as a fallback.
His deepest worry is **poorer streets** being policed by machines before anywhere else.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time for anyone to prepare.
He fears being **32 with no trade** once robots can walk his beat.
whatWouldHelp: A **written guarantee** that no officer is cut until robots are proven.
A paid **retraining fund** for officers who want to keep working with people.
